findings.source_quote: παρ’ οἷς δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ χάριτι ἠπίστατο ἀγνοούμενος
findings.english_quote: But among those whom he knew did not recognize the favor, he changed his appearance, so that he would neither distress them nor seem to act against the laws he himself had established.
findings.issue: The passive participle predicates being unrecognized or misunderstood of Zeus. The main English instead makes the favor itself the object of failed recognition. The note acknowledges the Greek construction, but does not make this change of object faithful to it.
findings.suggested_revision: Keep Zeus as the person not recognized or understood: for example, 'But among those who, he knew, did not recognize him in connection with the favor, he changed his appearance ...' Explain in the note the alternatives of his being unrecognized and his being misunderstood with respect to the favor. Review the revised wording afresh.

findings.source_quote: ὁ Ζεὺς αὐτὸς ὁ τούτων, νομοθέτης
findings.english_quote: Zeus himself, the lawgiver of these people
findings.issue: The English fixes τούτων as referring to people. That is a defensible contextual interpretation, but reference to the previously mentioned laws is also viable and materially changes the expressed relationship. No note discloses this choice.
findings.suggested_revision: Add a source-quoted note explaining the human antecedent chosen for 'these people' and preserving the alternative 'the lawgiver of these laws.' Treat this as referent ambiguity, not as a transcription defect.

findings.source_quote: ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Διὸς τοῦ πατρὸς θεῶν τε καὶ ἀνθρώπων ἄρξομαι τὰς ἐνίων μηνύειν κοινωνίας
findings.english_quote: I will begin with Zeus himself, the father of gods and humans, and disclose some of his unions
findings.issue: The Zeus-centered wording is contextually defensible, but τὰς ἐνίων κοινωνίας literally concerns the unions 'of/with some,' with an unstated referent for ἐνίων. It can concern some of the divine beings under discussion, or certain partners in Zeus's unions. The draft silently converts this into a selection of his unions and supplies no explanation or alternative.
findings.suggested_revision: Add a source-quoted note comparing the main wording with 'I will begin with Zeus himself ... and disclose the unions of some of them.' Explain that the main rendering follows the immediate focus on Zeus, while preserving both the possible divine referent and the reading 'unions with some [partners].' Any replacement main text requires fresh review.

findings.source_quote: Καλλιστοῖ τῇ Λυκάονος ἠγριώθη λέων, καὶ ἄλλον τίκτει Ἀρκάδα
findings.english_quote: For Callisto, daughter of Lycaon, he became a fierce lion, and she bears another, Arcas.
findings.issue: Callisto is a defensible inferred subject of τίκτει, but the subject is not expressed. Continuing Zeus as the subject is also viable, since τίκτω can describe a male begetting offspring. The existing note identifies the inference but does not preserve this material alternative.
findings.suggested_revision: Expand the note to preserve 'and he begets another, Arcas' as the alternative that continues Zeus as subject. Explain that the main text instead infers Callisto from the childbearing context and therefore assumes an unmarked subject change. The ambiguity does not itself require blocking publication.

findings.source_quote: μηδὲ τῶν ἀρρένων τὰς μίξεις φυλασσομένων ὡς αἰσχράς, ἀλλὰ ἐπιτηδευόντων καὶ τοῦτο ὡς εὐπρεπές.
findings.english_quote: They do not even avoid unions with males as shameful, but practice this too as something becoming.
findings.issue: After the preceding clause about 'foolish people,' the English pronoun 'They' has a competing antecedent that can wrongly attribute these practices to those people. The Greek participles continue the account of the gods and their unions.
findings.suggested_revision: Make the intended subject explicit: 'The gods do not even avoid unions with males as shameful, but practice this too as something becoming.' Review that replacement in context.
